extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of drama/literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, recognition, spectacle, and stagecraft) aimed at producing the proper tragic effects of pity and fear. Focuses on plot construction, types of recognition, character requirements, and practical composition/staging rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition, then, being between persons, it may happen that one person only is recognised by the other—when the latter is already known—or it may be necessary that the recognition should be on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognitions may be one-sided or mutual; the poet must decide which is required by the plot. Examples: Iphigenia revealed to Orestes by a letter (one-sided), but Orestes must also be made known to Iphigenia by another act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and Recognition should depend on surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Two parts, then, of the Plot—Reversal of the Situation and Recognition—turn upon surprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unexpected reversals and recognitions to produce the emotional effects of pity and fear. Surprise is the operative mechanism for these dramatic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include incidents that are genuinely destructive/painful when the plot requires it; their placement and causal role must serve to arouse pity and fear rather than mere sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The separate parts into which Tragedy is divided—namely, Prologue, Episode, Exodos, Choric song; this last being divided into Parodos and Stasimon. The Prologos is that entire part of a tragedy which precedes the Parodos of the Chorus. The Episode is that entire part of a tragedy which is between complete choric songs. The Exodos is that entire part of a tragedy which has no choric song after it. Of the Choric part the Parodos is the first undivided utterance of the Chorus,; the Stasimon is a Choric ode without anapaests; the Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standardized parts and their functions in structuring the play. Note also that songs of actors and commoi are peculiar features to some plays; observe conventions (where present).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should be complex (not simple) and imitate actions that excite pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan. It should, moreover, imitate actions which excite pity and fear, this being the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select plot situations that naturally generate pity and fear (not merely moral shock). The complexity (complication + unravelling) is necessary to produce the proper tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune: right kind (good to bad by error)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune presented must not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity ... Nor should the downfall of the utter villain be exhibited. There remains, then, the character between these two extremes,—that of a man who is not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice, but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist of high standing who falls from good fortune to bad by hamartia (error/frailty). Avoid virtuous→adversity (which shocks but arouses neither pity nor fear) and the downfall of absolute villains (which arouses moral satisfaction but neither pity nor fear). Examples: Oedipus, Thyestes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot: single issue preferred to double
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should, therefore, be single in its issue, rather than double as some maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single, unified storyline that culminates in one principal catastrophe rather than splitting the audience's sympathy with opposing conclusions; double plots may gratify weak spectators but are inferior for true tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character requirements: goodness, propriety, likeness, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character there are four things to be aimed at. First ... it must be good. Second ... propriety (what is fitting). Thirdly, character must be true to life (likeness). Fourth ... consistency (even the inconsistent must be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters have morally intelligible aims (goodness relative to their class), possess traits appropriate to their role (propriety), behave in ways believable by necessity or probability (likeness), and remain internally consistent. Anti-patterns: motiveless degradation (Menelaus in Orestes), inappropriate speeches/acts (lament of Odysseus, Melanippe's speech), inconsistency of Iphigenia at Aulis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of traits to role
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a type of manly valour; but valour in a woman, or unscrupulous cleverness, is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign traits that suit the character's social/sexual/role type; exceptional traits are possible but must be justified so they do not appear wholly out of place or general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality: use necessity or probability; avoid irrational/unmotivated elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should always aim either at the necessary or the probable ... the unravelling of the plot, no less than the complication, must arise out of the plot itself; it must not be brought about by the Deus ex Machina — The Deus ex Machina should be employed only for events external to the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure events follow by necessity or likely sequence from what precedes; avoid deus ex machina to resolve the play's central action (it may be acceptable only for antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge). Examples of misuse: Medea and the Return of the Greeks in the Iliad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of recognition modes: preference for natural/incidental recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition: by signs (congenital or acquired), by tokens, by memory (sight/hearing), by process of reasoning, and artifices invented by poet. The best recognitions are those arising from the incidents themselves; tokens and formal proofs are less artistic; poet-invented recognitions are poorest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that naturally emerge from the plot (e.g., Oedipus' recognition by the course of events, Iphigenia by a timely letter). Use memory or reasoning secondarily; tokens, external signs and poet-invented declarations are less artful and should be used sparingly. Examples: Odysseus' scar (tokens used with art), Orestes/Iphigenia (letters), contrived examples like 'voice of the shuttle' are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invented/self-revealed recognitions when unwarranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet (e.g., a character declaring 'I am X' because the poet wants it) are nearly allied to the fault of artificial proof and are wanting in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have characters announce identities or manufacture recognitions that the plot does not require; such moves are artistically weak and akin to using tokens for proof rather than letting the incident itself effect recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of horrific deeds and recognitions (best/worst cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only four possible ways: (1) do the deed knowing, (2) do it in ignorance and discover afterwards, (3) be about to act knowing the persons and then not act (worst), (4) be about to act through ignorance and recognise before acting (best).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most effective tragic arrangements are (a) the deed committed in ignorance with recognition after (startling effect), and (b) the almost-committed deed where recognition occurs in time to prevent it (best). Avoid the situation where the person knows and refrains—this is shocking but not truly tragic since no disaster follows. Examples: Merope at Cresphontes, Iphigenia, Sophocles' Oedipus, Antigone/Haemon example for near-action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear via plot, not merely spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way... Those who employ spectacular means to create a sense not of the terrible but only of the monstrous are strangers to the purpose of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely primarily on the plot's construction to produce pity and fear; do not substitute graphic or monstrous spectacle for genuine tragic effect. Spectacle is secondary and requires theatrical resources; the superior poet achieves the effect even when the tale is only heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization, staging and natural gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes ... the poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures; for those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes as if seeing them enacted to catch stage feasibilities and avoid inconsistencies (the Carcinus example). Design gestures and actions that are natural to the emotion being represented (agitated people should act agitated, anger should rage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition method: outline then episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the story, whether the poet takes it ready made or constructs it for himself, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a clear general plan (the overall situation and recognition/reversal points), then compose concise episodes that are relevant and connected to the main action; episodes in drama are short and should be appropriate to the overall design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and relevance of episodes; désis and lysis (complication and resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has the binding (dèsis) and the release (lysis). I mean by dèsis the part from the beginning up to the point from which change to good or bad fortune happens; by lysis that from the point of reversal to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the plot so that the complication (dèsis) leads inevitably to the reversal and resolution (lysis). Keep incidental episodes relevant to these arcs. In drama, episodes should be brief; the epic or narrative elements may be longer when outside the action proper.
